triplets.tail: Lead proponent; submitted formal proposal January 2019; Council mandate supports establishment of full-fledged permanent multilateral investment court

triplets.head: EU
triplets.tail: Only a permanent standing institution with full-time professional judges and appeal can ensure independence, impartiality, consistency, and diversity

triplets.head: EU
triplets.tail: CETA Art. 8.29, EU-Vietnam IPA, EU-Singapore IPA, EU-Mexico modernized agreement all include transitional MIC clauses

triplets.head: European Parliament
triplets.tail: Multiple resolutions endorsing the MIC initiative

triplets.head: Council of the EU
triplets.tail: Formal mandate supporting MIC establishment

triplets.head: Latin American states
triplets.tail: Generally supportive of ambitious reform; often intervene calling for more ambitious reform than incremental fixes

triplets.head: Bahrain
triplets.tail: Unequivocally expressed concern that limiting deliberations to procedural issues would be a missed opportunity

triplets.head: United States
triplets.tail: Skeptical; prefers incremental procedural fixes; has never submitted a formal proposal supporting MIC

triplets.head: United States
triplets.tail: Traditional party-appointed arbitration model works; replacing it with state-controlled court risks undermining investor confidence

triplets.head: Japan
triplets.tail: Cautious; uncertain about merit of rushing towards radical reforms; prefers improving existing system

triplets.head: Canada
triplets.tail: Pragmatic middle ground; co-designed CETA ICS with EU but at UNCITRAL aligns more with US/Japan/UK on incremental reforms

triplets.head: United Kingdom
triplets.tail: Leans incremental; aligns with US-Japan-Singapore group

triplets.head: Singapore
triplets.tail: Cautious; reform process should not be prejudiced in favor of MIC; strong interest in maintaining position as arbitration hub

triplets.head: China
triplets.tail: Hybrid approach: supports permanent appellate mechanism but preserves right of parties to appoint first-instance arbitrators

triplets.head: China
triplets.tail: July 2019 proposal supporting study of permanent appellate body, mediation, mandatory pre-arbitration consultations, third-party funding transparency

triplets.head: China
triplets.tail: Right to appoint arbitrators is a fundamental feature of international arbitration and should be retained

triplets.head: China
triplets.tail: Reform process should not be prejudiced in favor of MIC; different states may need different solutions

triplets.head: China
triplets.tail: Straddles divide between structural and incremental reform; may represent current temperature of negotiating room

triplets.head: Russia
triplets.tail: Opposed to structural reform; consistently downplayed need for public law measures such as transparency and multilateral investment courts

triplets.head: Russia
triplets.relation: view on party appointment of arbitrators
triplets.tail: Right to choose and appoint an arbitrator is inherent to the legitimacy of an arbitral award; reform of this is irrational and unreasonable

triplets.head: Russia
triplets.tail: Not a systemic flaw but a natural feature of treaty-based system; divergent outcomes expected since each BIT is unique

triplets.head: Russia
triplets.tail: Reform agenda driven by subjective perceptions rather than evidence; no persuasive reason to design global solutions to a local concern

triplets.head: South Korea
triplets.tail: Cautious; reform process should not be prejudiced in favor of MIC; called for capacity building and balanced stakeholder inclusion

triplets.head: Vietnam
triplets.tail: Cautious at multilateral level; signed EU-Vietnam IPA with bilateral ICS showing pragmatic acceptance bilaterally

triplets.head: South Africa
triplets.tail: Openly critical; warned of risks of structural ISDS reform and creating new problems; prefers domestic courts

triplets.head: Indonesia
triplets.tail: Openly critical; warned of risks of structural ISDS reform; among most active BIT terminators (25+ terminations)

triplets.head: Israel
triplets.tail: Critical; called for more balanced stakeholder inclusion and capacity building

triplets.head: African states collectively
triplets.tail: Lukewarm — neither actively support nor formally oppose; deep structural concerns

triplets.head: African states
triplets.tail: MIC modeled on WTO Dispute Settlement Model under which African countries face prohibitive costs, lack of technical expertise, and unequal representation

triplets.head: African states
triplets.tail: MIC does not address fundamental imbalance in investment treaties (substantive protections without corresponding obligations)

triplets.head: African states
triplets.tail: MIC does not accommodate Africa's preference for non-binding, cooperative, prevention-based dispute resolution as reflected in PAIC

triplets.head: African states
triplets.tail: Unclear relationship between MIC and Africa's own regional mechanisms (AfCFTA DSM), risking fragmentation

triplets.head: African states
triplets.tail: MIC could represent EU hegemony — multilateralizing EU's preferred architecture

triplets.head: India
triplets.tail: Ambivalent; pursues its own radical model (2015 Model BIT); MIC may be unnecessary if strong domestic courts and local remedies exhaustion in place

triplets.head: Brazil
triplets.tail: Implicit opponent; pursues entirely different CFIA paradigm based on dispute prevention rather than adjudication

triplets.head: White Industries v. India (2011)
triplets.tail: India liable for denial of justice (11-year delay in courts); investor imported 'effective means' obligation from India-Kuwait BIT via MFN clause in India-Australia BIT

triplets.head: White Industries v. India (2011)
triplets.tail: Led India to terminate ~58 BITs starting 2016 and adopt radically restrictive 2015 India Model BIT eliminating FET, omitting MFN, requiring 5-year local remedies

triplets.head: Pope & Talbot v. Canada (2001)
triplets.tail: FET is an additive standard going beyond CIL minimum standard of treatment

triplets.head: Pope & Talbot v. Canada (2001)
triplets.tail: Directly triggered NAFTA FTC Interpretive Note (July 2001) binding FET to CIL minimum standard; influenced 2004 US Model BIT Art. 5

triplets.tail: NAFTA Art. 1105 prescribes the customary international law minimum standard of treatment and does not require treatment in addition to or beyond CIL

triplets.head: Metalclad v. Mexico (2000)
triplets.tail: Contributed to NAFTA FTC Note; influenced inclusion of detailed expropriation annexes in 2004 US Model BIT

triplets.head: Ethyl Corp. v. Canada (1998)
triplets.tail: Directly influenced inclusion of Annex B regulatory carve-out in 2004 US Model BIT for indirect expropriation

triplets.head: Philip Morris v. Uruguay (2016) and Philip Morris v. Australia (2015)
triplets.tail: Accelerated trend of including right to regulate clauses in new-generation treaties; chilling-effect concern drove reform

triplets.head: Argentine crisis cases (CMS, LG&E, Enron)
triplets.tail: Led to more nuanced general exception clauses modeled on GATT Art. XX and explicit essential security exceptions

triplets.head: CME v. Czech Republic (2001)

triplets.head: ISDS reform typology - Tier 1
triplets.tail: Optimization (Incremental/Procedural Reform)

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1a
triplets.tail: Procedural refinement: improve transparency, speed, cost-effectiveness of existing arbitration

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1a
triplets.tail: UNCITRAL Transparency Rules (2014), ICSID Rule Amendments (2022), codes of conduct for arbitrators

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1a
triplets.tail: US, Japan, UK, Singapore, Russia

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1b
triplets.tail: Substantive clarification: tighten treaty language to constrain arbitral discretion

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1b
triplets.tail: FET tied to CIL; indirect expropriation annexes; MFN exclusion of ISDS; regulatory carve-outs

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1b
triplets.tail: US Model BIT (2012), RCEP

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1c
triplets.tail: Frivolous claim filters: mechanisms to dismiss meritless claims early

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 1 - Subtype 1d
triplets.tail: Roster/pool systems: replace full party appointment with selection from pre-approved rosters

triplets.head: ISDS reform typology - Tier 2
triplets.tail: Replacement (Systemic/Structural Reform)

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2a
triplets.tail: Bilateral investment courts: two-party permanent court with standing judges

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2a
triplets.tail: CETA ICS, EU-Vietnam IPA, EU-Singapore IPA

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2a
triplets.tail: EU (as transitional step)

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2b
triplets.tail: Multilateral investment court: global standing tribunal with tenured judges + appellate body

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2b
triplets.tail: UNCITRAL Standing Mechanism draft statute

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2b
triplets.tail: EU + 27 Member States

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2c
triplets.tail: Standalone appellate mechanism: add appeal layer on top of existing ad hoc first-instance arbitration

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2c
triplets.tail: China, some developing states

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2d
triplets.tail: Regional courts: create regional investment dispute bodies

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 2 - Subtype 2d
triplets.tail: Proposed AfCFTA AIRDS, OHADA CCJA, proposed ASEAN mechanism

triplets.head: ISDS reform typology - Tier 3
triplets.tail: Abolition (Paradigmatic Reform)

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3a
triplets.tail: Domestic court primacy: replace ISDS with domestic courts + possible state-to-state arbitration

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3a
triplets.tail: South Africa Protection of Investment Act (2015), India Model BIT (5-year local remedies)

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3a
triplets.tail: South Africa, India

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3b
triplets.tail: Dispute prevention/ombudsman model: replace adversarial adjudication with cooperative prevention mechanisms

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3b
triplets.tail: Brazil CFIA

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3b
triplets.tail: Brazil

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3c
triplets.tail: Full treaty termination: terminate BITs without replacement; rely on domestic law only

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3c
triplets.tail: Bolivia withdrew from ICSID 2007 and terminated all BITs; Ecuador terminated 12 BITs and withdrew from ICSID 2009; Venezuela withdrew from ICSID 2012

triplets.head: ISDS reform Tier 3 - Subtype 3d
triplets.tail: Intra-regional termination: terminate BITs within a specific regional bloc

triplets.tail: EU Termination Agreement (2020): 23 Member States terminated all intra-EU BITs

triplets.head: Comparison matrix key dimension 1
triplets.tail: Level of FET restrictiveness: US/RCEP anchor to CIL → CETA closed list → India eliminates FET → Brazil omits entirely

triplets.head: Comparison matrix key dimension 2
triplets.tail: Treatment of indirect expropriation: US/CETA/RCEP factor-based + carve-outs → India police powers → Brazil eliminates indirect expropriation

triplets.head: Comparison matrix key dimension 3
triplets.tail: MFN scope control: US negative lists → CETA/RCEP explicitly exclude ISDS → India eliminates MFN altogether

triplets.head: Comparison matrix key dimension 4
triplets.tail: ISDS architecture: US traditional ad hoc → CETA permanent court → RCEP defers → India restricts with 5-year exhaustion → Brazil eliminates ISDS

triplets.head: Comparison matrix key dimension 5
triplets.tail: Investor obligations: US/RCEP none → CETA limited references → India/Brazil explicit substantive obligations

triplets.head: MIC debate three-way split
triplets.tail: EU bloc: wants permanent standing multilateral court to replace ad hoc arbitration entirely

triplets.head: MIC debate three-way split
triplets.tail: Improve-not-replace coalition (US, Japan, UK, Canada, Singapore, Russia): retain ad hoc arbitration but improve it

triplets.head: MIC debate three-way split
triplets.tail: Reject-the-premise coalition (South Africa, Brazil, India, Indonesia, many African states): question whether any form of international investor-state adjudication is desirable; prefer domestic courts, ombudsmen, or dispute prevention

triplets.head: Causal chain feedback loop
triplets.tail: Broad treaty language → expansive arbitral interpretation → state backlash → restrictive treaty redrafting → more predictable interpretation → further refinement

triplets.head: Pan-African Investment Code (PAIC)
triplets.tail: Binding investor obligations, counterclaims by host states, preference for non-binding cooperative dispute resolution
